title: Crypto wallets: the best and most secure options
h1: Crypto wallets: which to use, and how to set them up safely
seo_title: Best and most secure crypto wallets compared: hardware, software, multisig and MPC
description: Hardware, software, multisig and seedless wallets compared on chains, open source, security features, incidents and cost, plus a 10-step security setup.
summary: Hardware, hot, multisig and seedless wallets compared, with sourced incidents and a 10-step safe setup.
plain: A crypto wallet doesn't hold coins. It holds the keys that prove the coins are yours. Whoever has your seed phrase (the 12 or 24 backup words) owns your crypto.

A hardware wallet keeps the keys on a small device, offline. A software or 'hot' wallet keeps them on your phone or computer, which is handy but easier to attack. Most people should use both: hardware for savings, hot for spending.
dont_lose: Never share your seed phrase. No real support team will ever ask for it.
Buy hardware wallets only from the maker's own store.
Keep savings in a wallet that never connects to new sites.
Check the address and amount on the device screen before you approve.
Use a small burner wallet for memecoins and new sites.
risk: Wallet facts were checked Oct 26-27, 2026 and can change. No wallet protects you if you sign a malicious transaction or give away your seed. Not financial advice; no strategy wins every trade.

items: Hardware (cold)
A device that keeps keys offline and signs on its own screen. Best for savings.
Software (hot)
A phone app or browser extension. Fast and free, but exposed to malware and phishing. Best for trading money.
Multisig
Needs several keys to approve a transaction. Best for large sums or shared funds.
MPC and smart wallets
No single seed phrase. The key is split up, or you sign in with a passkey. Easier for beginners, but you rely on the provider's recovery.

items.name: Ledger
items.summary: The best-known hardware wallet maker. Keys sit in a certified secure-element chip.
glance: From $69 (Nano S Plus); other models $99-$399. Checked Oct 26, 2026
Thousands of coins and tokens across major chains
Ledger Wallet app yes (MIT); the secure-element OS is closed
lists: Beginners who want a widely supported device
The closed secure-element code, and the optional Ledger Recover service, are a matter of trust

facts.text: July 2020: Ledger's e-commerce database leaked. About 1M emails and about 272,000 full names, addresses and phone numbers were later dumped, which led to years of phishing mail aimed at owners. Seeds were not exposed.

src.label: Ledger, July 2020 e-commerce data breach

facts.text: Dec 14, 2023: a malicious version of Ledger's Connect Kit code library was pushed to apps that used it, and drained about $600K from users who signed on affected dapps. The devices themselves were not breached.

src.label: Ledger, Connect Kit security incident report

facts.text: Oct 2026: Ledger confirmed that devices sold by a Southeast Asian reseller carried a hidden implant that captured the recovery phrase during setup and sent it out over mobile data. Ledger says its chip, OS and servers were not compromised. It asked resellers in the region to suspend sales and tightened handling rules.

src.label: BleepingComputer, Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts

facts.text: Ledger called it a 'localized distribution attack' and said spot checks of stock elsewhere found no tampered units.

src.label: Ledger, response to the hardware implant attack

items.name: Trezor
items.summary: The original hardware wallet, with fully open-source firmware. Newer Safe models add a secure element.
glance: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and many others
lists: Users who want to verify the code
Buy direct: Trezor is ending reseller authorisations on Jan 1, 2027
Never use a device that arrives with a seed already written down

facts.text: Safe 5 uses an EAL6+ certified secure element (Infineon OPTIGA Trust M). Safe 7 adds an auditable TROPIC01 chip and is marketed as quantum-ready.

src.label: Trezor, secure elements in Trezor Safe devices

facts.text: Jan 2024: an attacker got into a third-party support ticketing portal, exposing contact details of up to 66,000 users. Trezor said no seeds or devices were affected and warned about follow-up phishing.

src.label: Trezor blog, security alert on phishing

facts.text: Oct 13, 2026: Trezor told resellers their authorisation ends on Jan 1, 2027, calling it a precaution after the Ledger implant case. It said there was no evidence its own devices were compromised.

src.label: Decrypt, Trezor cuts its resellers after Ledger finds spy implant

items.name: Tangem
items.summary: NFC cards that tap against your phone. It can work without a written seed phrase, using 2-3 backup cards instead.
glance: App yes; card firmware audited but not updatable
lists: Beginners who fear losing a paper seed
Losing every card means losing access, so store backups in separate places

facts.text: Tangem uses an EAL6+ Samsung chip. Its card code was audited by Kudelski Security in 2018.

src.label: Tangem help centre, Tangem and security

items.name: Keystone 3 Pro
items.summary: Never connects by USB or Bluetooth. It talks to your phone or computer only through QR codes.
glance: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and more, via MetaMask, Rabby, Solflare and others
Firmware on GitHub; some libraries are precompiled
lists: Pairing with a software wallet you already use
QR signing is slower, so it's not for fast memecoin trading

facts.text: Keystone 3 Pro uses three secure elements, and its firmware is published on GitHub.

src.label: Keystone, open source and transparency

items.name: Phantom
items.summary: The most popular Solana wallet, now multichain. It has built-in swaps and transaction warnings.
glance: Solana, Ethereum, Base, Polygon, Bitcoin, BNB Chain, HyperEVM and others (no Arbitrum or Optimism)
lists: It's a hot wallet, so keep savings elsewhere

facts.text: Phantom's supported networks are listed in its help centre; Arbitrum, Optimism and Avalanche are not among them.

src.label: Phantom help, supported networks

facts.text: Walletbeat lists Phantom's source code as not openly licensed.

src.label: Walletbeat, Phantom profile

items.name: MetaMask
items.summary: The default Ethereum wallet. It added Solana in May 2025 and Bitcoin in Dec 2025.
glance: Free; optional Transaction Shield $9.99/mo. Checked Oct 26, 2026
lists: Pairing with Ledger, Trezor or Keystone
Fake MetaMask extensions are common, so install only from metamask.io

facts.text: MetaMask's licence is source-available but not open source in the usual sense.

src.label: MetaMask extension licence on GitHub

facts.text: Oct 2026: researchers found a phishing campaign that abused a flaw on MetaMask's real Portfolio site to show a fake 'verify your wallet' notice asking for the seed phrase. MetaMask fixed it by Oct 19. Nothing legitimate ever asks for your seed.

src.label: Kauz Security, content injection on portfolio.metamask.io

items.name: Rabby
items.summary: An open-source EVM wallet that simulates every transaction before you sign and shows its risks.
lists: Anyone worried about drainers and approvals

facts.text: Rabby offers pre-sign transaction simulation and a built-in approvals manager.

src.label: Rabby, security

items.name: Solflare
items.summary: A Solana-only wallet with transaction simulation and support for Ledger and Keystone.
lists: Using a hardware wallet on Solana

items.name: Backpack
items.summary: A wallet from the team behind the Backpack exchange. It covers Solana, Ethereum and others, and supports Ledger, Trezor and Keystone.
lists: Solana plus EVM in one wallet
Linked to an exchange brand, so check you have the real download

items.name: Base App (formerly Coinbase Wallet)
items.summary: Coinbase Wallet became the Base App in July 2025. Base Account uses passkeys (your phone's face or fingerprint login) instead of a seed phrase.
lists: Recovery depends on your passkey and cloud account, so secure those well

facts.text: Coinbase describes the move from Coinbase Wallet to the Base App.

src.label: Base blog, A new day one (Coinbase Wallet becomes the Base App)

items.name: Safe
items.summary: A multisig needs M of N keys (for example 2 of 3) to approve a transaction, so one stolen key is not enough.
lists: Teams, treasuries and large personal holdings
Every signer must check what they sign on their own device

facts.text: Feb 21, 2025: about $1.5B was stolen from Bybit. The FBI attributed it to North Korea. Investigators found malicious JavaScript in Safe's web interface that showed signers a harmless-looking transaction. Lesson: check the transaction on the hardware device screen, not just the website.

src.label: FBI PSA: North Korea responsible for $1.5 billion Bybit hack

items.name: Squads
lists: The same 'verify what you sign' rule as Safe

facts.text: Squads Protocol v4 was audited by OtterSec, Neodyme, Certora and Trail of Bits, and formally verified.

src.label: Squads docs, Protocol v4 security audits

items.name: Zengo
items.summary: MPC splits your key into parts held on your phone and on Zengo's servers, so there is no seed phrase to steal.
lists: Beginners who don't want a seed phrase
You depend on the company's servers and recovery process

facts.text: Zengo describes its MPC, seedless security model.

src.label: Zengo, security model

items: 1. Split hot and cold
Cold wallet (hardware): your savings. It never connects to new sites. Hot wallet (Phantom, Rabby and similar): only what you are trading this week.
2. Add a burner
A third wallet with a small balance for new sites, mints, claims and memecoins. If it gets drained, you lose only that small balance.
3. Buy hardware direct
Order only from the maker's official store. Never buy second-hand, from marketplaces, or a 'cheap' unit. Tampered devices look and work normally.
4. Make your own seed
Generate the seed phrase on the device yourself. Reject any device that comes with a seed card already filled in or a scratch-off PIN.
5. Store the seed offline
Write it on paper or metal and keep it in two safe places. Never photograph it, type it, store it in the cloud or a password manager, or send it to anyone.
6. Check the screen
Always confirm the address and amount on the hardware wallet's own screen before approving.
7. Simulate before you sign
Use a wallet that previews what will leave your wallet. If the preview is unclear or shows an unlimited approval, reject it.
8. Revoke monthly
Review and revoke old token approvals with revoke.cash or your wallet's approvals tool.
9. Lock down the rest
Use an authenticator app or a security key rather than SMS, set a SIM/port-out PIN with your carrier, and use a separate email for crypto.
10. Save addresses
Keep an address book of your own and trusted addresses. Never copy an address from your transaction history.

items.label: Scam guide: fake apps and tampered hardware

items.text: Aug 2022: Slope wallet's error-logging service recorded users' seed phrases. About $4.1M was drained from 9,231 Solana wallets. Lesson: one leaked seed can empty every chain that seed controls.

src.label: Solana Foundation, Aug 2, 2022 application wallet incident

items.text: June 2023: at least $35M was stolen from Atomic Wallet users. Elliptic attributed it to North Korea's Lazarus Group.

src.label: Elliptic, Lazarus likely behind $35 million Atomic Wallet theft

items.text: Dec 24, 2025: Trust Wallet's browser extension v2.68 was compromised. About 2,520 wallets were hit, the fix was v2.69, and Trust Wallet began reimbursing.

src.label: Trust Wallet, browser extension v2.68 incident update

items.text: Oct 17, 2026: attackers hijacked a notification provider used by NGRAVE's LIQUID app and sent a fake security alert linking to a copycat site that asked for the recovery phrase. NGRAVE traced about $2.56M stolen. The ZERO device itself was not breached.

src.label: NGRAVE, incident report: the fake LIQUID security alert
